nameStory: The name 'quahog' comes from the Narragansett Native American word 'poquauhock,' which referred to this hard-shelled clam. Early European colonists adopted this indigenous term, and it stuck so well that even today New Englanders proudly call them quahogs while much of the rest of the country knows them as hard clams. The scientific name 'Mercenaria' refers to their historical use as currency - Native Americans made wampum (shell money) from quahog shells.
description: The Northern Quahog is a chunky, oval-shaped clam with a thick, heavy shell that feels solid as a rock in your hands. These marine bivalves can grow as large as your fist, with shells typically ranging from 2-4 inches across. The outside of the shell is usually grayish-white to tan, often with darker growth rings that look like tree rings, while the inside gleams white with a distinctive purple edge where Native Americans once carved wampum beads. They're the clams that end up in New England clam chowder and stuffies!

idTips.label: Shell thickness and weight
idTips.description: Pick one up and feel its substantial heft - quahog shells are notably thick and heavy, feeling almost stone-like compared to other clams, earning them the name 'hard clam'

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Look for an oval to rounded triangular shape that's wider than it is tall, with a slightly flattened appearance rather than being perfectly round

idTips.label: Growth rings
idTips.description: Run your finger across the shell surface to feel the concentric ridges that mark each year's growth, like reading the rings of a tree

idTips.label: Interior purple coloring
idTips.description: Open shells reveal a bright white interior with a distinctive purple or deep violet band along the inner edge - this purple section was prized for making wampum

idTips.label: Shell color and texture
idTips.description: The exterior ranges from chalky white to gray or tan, sometimes with a yellowish tinge, and feels rough and chalky to the touch rather than smooth

habitat: Northern Quahogs burrow in sandy and muddy bottoms of shallow coastal waters throughout New England, from just below the low tide line down to about 50 feet deep. You'll find them in protected bays, estuaries, and tidal flats where the water is brackish to fully salty, often alongside soft-shell clams and blue mussels. Look for their shells washed up on beaches after storms, or spot the small holes they make in the sand when they extend their feeding tubes.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells begin washing up on beaches as storms subside, and this is when commercial clamming season typically begins as the clams become more active in warming waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding quahogs, both in their natural habitat and at seafood markets - they're actively feeding and easier to harvest in the warmer months.
seasonality.fall: Still active and commonly harvested through autumn, with shells continuing to wash ashore after fall storms provide good beachcombing opportunities.
seasonality.winter: Quahogs burrow deeper and become less active in cold water, but their heavy shells are still the most common large clam shells found on winter beaches.

funFact: Quahogs are among the longest-living animals on Earth - some have been found to be over 200 years old, meaning there are quahogs alive today in New England waters that were already adults when the Declaration of Independence was signed!
confusionNotes: Don't confuse quahogs with ocean quahogs (Arctica islandica), which are rounder, usually have a dark black outer covering, and lack the purple interior coloring. Remember: if it's got that purple inner rim and feels like a heavy stone, it's a true quahog!
contextualKnowledge: Be aware that 'quahog' specifically refers to the Northern Quahog (Mercenaria mercenaria), while the 'ocean quahog' is actually a completely different species in a different family altogether. This naming confusion trips up many people, but true New England quahogs are the ones with the purple-edged shells that make the best chowder and have the deep cultural connection to Native American wampum.
compareHints: Since Northern Quahogs are the only species in their genus Mercenaria found in New England, compare them to their relatives in the Venus clam family. Unlike other venus clams, quahogs are notably heavier and thicker-shelled, with that distinctive purple interior edge that's absent in related species. They're also much larger than most other venus clams you'll encounter on New England shores.
